overview: The Xin dynasty was a brief interregnum when Wang Mang attempted radical reforms inspired by ancient Zhou ideals. His policies failed to address real economic problems and natural disasters, above all the Yellow River's change of course, and ended in widespread rebellion.

items.text: Wang Mang claims the Mandate of Heaven has transferred to him based on omens and classical precedents.
Reforms modeled on the ancient Zhou well-field system and ritual codes.
Private land ownership abolished; all land declared the king's fields, to be redistributed in equal shares. The order was withdrawn within three years.
The trade in slaves banned, though the ban was widely ignored.
State monopolies on salt, iron, coinage and liquor, and a bureau to lend to farmers and steady prices.
Wang Mang's failure discredited radical reform and strengthened conservative Confucianism.
His reign became a cautionary tale about ignoring economic realities for ideological purity.

fall.text: Rebel armies captured Chang'an in 23 CE and killed Wang Mang; a Han prince, Liu Xiu, restored the dynasty in 25 as Emperor Guangwu.

sources.title: Denis Twitchett and Michael Loewe (eds.), The Cambridge History of China, volume 1: The Ch'in and Han Empires (1986), chapter 3
